evidence.paraphrase: Vyāsa asks about Mukundā after hearing Rukmāṅgada’s ascent. She remains consumed by desire, abandons food/water and sleeps exhausted in the forest. Indra knows her longing, assumes Rukmāṅgada’s form and has intercourse with her; she returns home believing the prince was her partner. Indra vanishes. She conceives and bears a beautiful son in the ninth month.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Birth resounds through earth, sky and directions and startles birds. Vācaknavi leaves his daily rites and, unaware of Mukundā’s conduct, joyfully performs birth rites and donations. After ten days he names the child Gṛtsamada with astrologer Brahmin approval; in the fifth year initiates him and performs four Vedic vows. The boy learns from a single utterance. Vācaknavi, called father in this social/ritual setting, teaches the Vedic Gaṇānāṃ tvā mantra, prescribing steady Gaṇeśa contemplation for success and fame.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Gṛtsamada practices mantra/meditation. King Magadha of Magadha, generous, martial and learned, with two unnamed learned ministers and devoted curse/grace-capable wife Ambikā, hosts his father’s śrāddha. Invited sages include Vasiṣṭha and Atri, and Gṛtsamada. His boast in śāstra discussion provokes Atri’s rebuke: ascetic merit earns respect, but alleged birth from prince Rukmāṅgada excludes equal sage-honour. Gṛtsamada flares with rage, others flee, and he threatens to burn the sages by curse if he proves not Rukmāṅgada’s son.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Gṛtsamada demands his father’s identity and threatens to burn Mukundā if she refuses. Frightened, she admits longing for the hunting prince while husband Vācaknavi was practicing, and believes Rukmāṅgada his father. Ashamed and angry, the son curses her to be a thorny forest plant with countless fruits shunned by all living creatures.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Mukundā counters that her son disregarded motherhood: he will father a terrible mighty daitya frightening three worlds. She immediately abandons her body and becomes a forest badarī avoided even by birds. Heavenly speech reveals Gṛtsamada was born from Indra. He leaves for austerity. Hearing this account promises freedom from distress and fulfilment.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Gṛtsamada reaches flower-rich Puṣpaka forest, bows to resident sages and stays with permission. Bathing, he fixes mind on Gaṇeśa, stands on a toe, restrains senses/breath/self, looks toward nose-tip and takes air. After1,000 divine years, opened eyes emit fire distressing gods who fear whose office he seeks. He then subsists on one fallen leaf, immobile, for a further15,000 as stated (the later clause gives number without repeating years).
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Compassionate Gaṇeśa appears quickly, radiant, moon-browed, lion-mounted, ten-armed with serpent sacred cord and lotus garland, accompanied by Siddhi/Buddhi. His radiance overwhelms Gṛtsamada, who faints, resumes inward contemplation and fears his practice wasted; he begs rescue and recalls exclusion from sage honours. Gaṇeśa identifies himself as arriving for grace, praises toe-supported austerity and asks desired boon. The sage bows joyfully.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Weeping and dancing, Gṛtsamada calls birth/austerity fulfilled. By deity’s command he asks Brahman-knowledge and knowledge, firm devotion and unforgetting remembrance, supremacy among devotees, exclusive devotional standing able to draw three worlds, worldwide honour by gods/humans. He asks Puṣpaka forest/city fame as Gaṇeśapura, continued divine residence and fulfilment of devotees’ wishes.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Gaṇeśa affirms all requested things and grants rare Brahmin standing. Because he recited Gaṇānāṃ tvā, Gṛtsamada becomes that Vedic mantra’s ṛṣi; he gains supreme honour before Brahmā and Vasiṣṭha’s sages. Remembering him first then Gaṇeśa at undertakings yields success; ritual without deity/ṛṣi/metre knowledge is fruitless. A mighty famous son will terrify gods, be undefeatable by all except Rudra and remain Gaṇeśa-devoted. Site names are Puṣpaka in divine/Kṛta era as printed devayuga, Maṇipūra in Tretā, Bhānaka in Dvāpara and Bhadraka in Kali; bathing/giving there grants wishes.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.

evidence.paraphrase: Gaṇeśa vanishes after giving boons. Gṛtsamada installs his image, builds a fine temple, establishes enduring Varada name and worships devotedly. Site becomes a siddhi-place/Puṣpaka through divine favour. Listening to boon-account promises all wishes and firm Gaṇeśa devotion freeing transmigration.
evidence.verification_notes: Direct Sanskrit body reading; not independent edition verification. Uncertain Sanskrit clauses identified separately.
